### The Department of Unclaimed Things

On her third day at the Department of Unclaimed Things, Nora learned that a single glove was worth keeping for ninety days, but a pair of gloves only sixty.

“People come back for the single ones,” said Len, who had worked there since before the city put numbers on its bus stops. “They’ve got the other one at home reminding them.”

He showed her how to tag an umbrella without opening it and how to tell, by weight, whether a lunchbox needed immediate attention. At four he made tea in a kettle that had been left on the number nine bus in 2006. Its owner had never come, although Len had once received a call from a man who could describe the kettle perfectly but insisted he had lost it at sea.

“Could have been his,” Len said. “People are unreliable about where they’ve been.”

The department occupied two rooms beneath the central bus station. All day, buses shuddered overhead, stirring dust from the pipes. Nora had taken the job because her father had died in February, and by April she had discovered that she needed work with a very clear distinction between what had been done and what hadn’t. A thing was tagged or it wasn’t. Nobody asked her how she was doing unless she had lifted something heavy.

Her father’s apartment was still full. The landlord had given her until the end of the month to empty it. She had managed the refrigerator and one kitchen drawer. The drawer contained eight birthday candles, a screwdriver with a broken handle, and a takeout menu on which her father had written, in his square draftsman’s capitals, NO GOOD. She had thrown away the candles and the screwdriver, then taken the menu out of the trash.

One Tuesday, a woman came to the counter looking for a green bag.

“What was inside?” Nora asked.

“Another bag.”

“And inside that?”

“Nothing. I was on my way to buy potatoes.”

Nora fetched three green bags, none of them right. The woman looked relieved at the sight of the third, then disappointed when she touched it.

“Mine had a better handle,” she said. “I made it from the waistband of my husband’s trousers.”

Nora asked for a phone number.

“Don’t trouble yourself,” the woman said, and left.

That afternoon Nora found the bag tucked inside a folding shopping cart. Its handle had a buttonhole at one end. She set it under the counter. There was a shelf for things awaiting collection, but to put it there she would have needed a name.

On Thursday, Len brought in a loaf of bread.

“My daughter’s got into sourdough,” he said. “She talks about it like she’s having trouble with a horse.”

They ate slices at the counter with butter shaved off a cold block. Nora told him about the apartment. She hadn’t meant to, but he asked whether she wanted to take the rest of the loaf home, and she said there wasn’t room in the freezer. All the food people had brought her in February was still in there.

“How much time have you got?” he asked.

“Nine days.”

“I can bring my van on Sunday.”

She started to explain that most of the things weren’t ready to go. Len said Sunday was when he had the van. They could see what was ready then.

He arrived at nine with a stack of empty banana boxes. Nora had spent the previous evening making signs that said KEEP, DONATE, and RUBBISH. When she opened the door, he was holding two coffees and looking down at a small brass plate screwed into the doorframe. Her father had installed it to cover a hole where a chain lock had been.

“Nice work,” Len said.

Nora had passed that plate hundreds of times. She ran a thumb over it. One corner stood slightly proud of the wood.

They packed the books first. Her father had owned several books about canals and a paperback about how to win at blackjack. Nora opened that one and found an old bus ticket marking page seventeen.

“He took a bus to the casino once,” she said. “He came home with more money than he left with. A woman at the stop lent him five pounds for the fare and he walked home instead.”

“Did he pay her back?”

“He spent two Saturdays waiting for her at the stop.”

Len held the box open. Nora put the book in.

By noon, the apartment sounded different. From the kitchen she could hear Len drawing the tape across a box in the bedroom. She opened the refrigerator, forgetting she had already emptied it, and stood in the light from the little bulb. Then she unplugged it and propped the door open with a shoe.

On Monday, the woman came back.

“I thought you might,” Nora said, reaching beneath the counter.

The woman put both hands flat on the green bag. She pressed the buttonhole with her thumb.

“I’ve bought the potatoes already,” she said.

“You can still take it.”

“Oh, I know.” She looked up at Nora. “I’m trying to remember what else I need.”

They stood there while she thought. Above them a bus pulled out, and something in the ceiling gave its usual small knock.

“Onions,” the woman said at last. She folded the bag into a neat square and put it in her coat pocket.

That evening Nora took a screwdriver to the apartment. She undid the two screws in the brass plate and caught it in her palm. Behind it was a ragged hole, with a bright scrape where the chain had once pulled loose. She remembered that happening. She’d been twelve and angry, and had yanked the door open while her father was still telling her she couldn’t go out. He’d looked at the chain lying on the floor and said, with genuine interest, “Well, I wouldn’t have thought you could do that.”

She stood in the doorway for a minute. Then she fetched the shoe from the kitchen and used it to prop the front door while she carried the last box down. Afterward she came back up, screwed the plate into place, and locked the door. The new tenant would never need to know about the hole. Nora hoped that, sooner or later, they’d notice the brass.
